content:
This month marks 60 years in the bourbon industry for distilling legend Jim Rutledge. His claim to fame is bringing Four Roses Bourbon back to the United States after decades of only being sold in Japan and other foreign markets, a move that has earned him a venerated place among whiskey geeks. But since retiring from Four Roses in 2015 he’s continued to build his legacy, helping to launch numerous brands including Cream of Kentucky and Echoes of Oak, the latter of which he distilled at Castle & Key Distillery.

Over the last six decades, Rutledge has seen everything from computers replacing handwritten ledgers to extreme changes in demand, enduring a number of booms and busts in the market. He’s credited with rescuing Four Roses Bourbon from certain oblivion, and even retirement couldn’t stop him from continuing to shape the distilled spirits landscape in the U.S. The unwavering passion Rutledge has for bourbon continues to reverberate through the industry. Even after a lifetime working in bourbon, Rutledge takes every opportunity to work closely with distilling and to share his experience with those coming up in the industry.

The Seagram’s Days

In 1966, Rutledge took a job at Seagram’s Calvert Distillery on 7th Street Rd. in Louisville. After graduating from the University of Louisville and working at Sears for two years, he’d landed two offers: one at tobacco manufacturer Phillip Morris, where one of the perks was that he could smoke all the free cigarettes he wanted at lunch, and another at Seagram’s.

“I didn’t want to take the first job that was offered,” Rutledge recalls. “I was hoping to find something a little more interesting, and hopefully a career.”

He worked in research and development then as a case goods shipping supervisor, and eventually as a bottling line planner. Though he started gaining some experience in distillery production, he’d often get called back to bottling during the holiday rush. Back in those days, he says operators would use pencil marks on the valves to control the optimal temperature and flow on the stills, something that is controlled by computers now.

“But I never really had enough time to learn the distillery business,” he says.

In November of 1977, shortly after managing the transition to palletization in the warehouses, he was transferred to New York.

An Unexpected ‘Promotion’

“[One day] I snuck out [of work] about 20 minutes early to go bowling,” he recalls. “The guard stopped me as I was walking out the gate. He said, ‘Jim, the plant superintendent wants to see you.’ I said, ’Oh my gosh, how did he know I was leaving early?’ And so I walked down to his office carrying my bowling ball and sat down.”

The superintendent told him he was getting promoted to chief industrial engineer in New York. While that would ordinarily be cause for celebration, Rutledge was wary of the move, reluctant to uproot his family. But back in those days, he says, it was take the job or take a hike, so he took the job.

“I went bowling, and I bowled the worst game I’d ever had in my life,” he laughs.

He couldn’t sleep that night, envisioning never seeing a park or a softball field ever again. What’s more, by the time he got to New York the job title was changed from chief industrial engineer to assistant manager of the budgets and standards department.

He spent 15 years in New York working for Seagram’s, all the while pining for the production floor. Finally, in 1990, his reviewer asked if he was serious about wanting to go back to production, sharing that he would be retiring in the next couple of years and was looking for someone to head up the Four Roses Distillery in Kentucky.

Two years later he was called to a meeting in Louisville. The topic: returning to Kentucky to get back into the production side.

The Four Roses Years

Rutledge spent his first two years back in Kentucky in Cox’s Creek, turning the tiny bottling operation into the massive warehousing and bottling facility it is today. In November of 1994, Rutledge was slated to shift his focus to the Four Roses Distillery in Lawrenceburg, but he received some troubling news from the higher-ups at Seagram’s.

“They told me the quality, what comes off the still before it goes into a barrel, was so bad and had been so bad for about three and a half years that if it didn’t improve by summer shutdown the second week of June 1995, they would have to fire everybody at the distillery.”

At that time Four Roses Bourbon was only sold in foreign markets. In 1959 the brand had shifted its focus to international consumers, mainly Japan. The product called Four Roses that was for sale in the U.S. was a blended whiskey made in both Indiana and Maryland, and it was widely regarded as a bottom shelf product.

“The guy I was replacing stayed on through the end of the year,” Rutledge recalls. “I got to know the distillery operations and the people, the atmosphere at the time was just very, very caustic.”

Knowing that the distillery had no option other than to improve the quality, Rutledge remembers subtly pushing the distillery floor to refine its process. “Once everybody left for the day, I’d go over and spend the next shift entirely with the distillery operators, listening and learning,” he says. “I couldn’t tell anybody that the distillery was going to be shut down if we didn’t turn the quality around. I just told them I believe in quality and we’ve got to improve”

He’d arrive each day around 7 a.m. to prepare for the morning shift to start at 8 a.m. He’d walk through the distillery at least three times a day, getting to know everyone from clerical to maintenance. He wanted to get a feel for how things worked, what wasn’t working, and where improvements could be made, and for him that meant starting with the people.

“I remember one of the guys saying, ‘You know, all you management guys say that, but none of you ever mean it.’ And I said, ‘You’ll see.’”

“One of the things that he told me was to go talk to the guy that’s been running the still for 20 years and see what you could learn,” says master blender Ashley Barnes, who worked with Rutledge at Four Roses and is now an industry consultant. “He was always ready to share his knowledge and teach me something, and willing to be patient and answer all my questions. I started working with Jim in 2014, and full circle is I’m getting to work with him again on Jacob Spears.”

Rutledge says there was a rigid structure to a union shop, so much so that if he walked into the distillery and a valve needed to be turned he could not turn it himself — he’d have to find someone in maintenance to do it. But that’s precisely why he felt he needed to learn the system so fully, because everyone’s success depended on it.

“That’s the kind of atmosphere I’ve always believed in, working together. I felt like they might report to me, but I worked for them.”

Seagram’s had a ratings system for new make distillate that ranged from one to five, one being the worst and five being the best. For the last three plus years before Rutledge got to Four Roses the average score was one. By the third week of January of 1995, Rutledge was sending then plant manager Al Young up to the Seagram’s distillery in Lawrenceburg, Ind. with distillate samples almost daily for evaluation by Jim Warner and Pat Loach.

Rutledge was averaging 16 to 18 hours a day when the call finally came. “Jim said, ‘Guys, what are you doing down there? This is unbelievable. I haven’t smelled a distillate like this in years!’ And my heart jumped. But then he laughed and said, ‘I just wanted to call you and let you know you just had your first four-rated quality in over three years.’”

But the brand wasn’t out of the woods yet. Number crunchers in the parent company had all but decided that it would be a huge cost-savings measure to shut it down. The majority of what the Four Roses Distillery was doing at that point was making blending whiskey for Seagram’s Seven Crown domestically and Crown Royal Seagram VO in Canada, and they certainly had plenty of other facilities that could make it. Fortunately the corporate quality department stepped in and said we can’t afford to lose Four Roses because the quality is too good.

Rutledge and his team had done it. He was awarded the Seagram’s Top Quality Award. He tried to share the prize with the union stewards but was denied, so instead bought everyone at the distillery matching Four Roses jean jackets and used the remaining funds to stock the vending machines in the break rooms.

Changing the Course of Four Roses History

At this point Four Roses Bourbon still was mainly sold in Japan, but Rutledge was determined to bring it to U.S. markets. “When I got back to Kentucky, it became a burning passion to get Four Roses back in the United States. I didn’t hesitate. I pushed people. I would talk to people, directors of marketing and sales, all the time. If they called me about something I always managed to steer the conversation toward getting Four Roses back in the United States.”

He managed to get the Four Roses Single Barrel on the market in 20 states by 1999. And in 2002, when Kirin took over the business from Seagram’s, Rutledge finally got a chance to make his big move.

The first week of January 2002, the CEO and CFO of Four Roses as well as representatives from Kirin spent a week in Lawrenceburg at the distillery. ”At the end of the week they said, ‘Jim-san, we’ve been asking questions of you all week. Do you have any questions for us?’” Of course, the first thing he thought of was to try to remove the legacy Seagram’s blended whiskey from the lineup and bring the Four Roses bourbon home to the U.S. To Rudlege’s pleasant surprise, they accepted the idea. “It was years later one of the Kirin personnel told me, ‘Jim, they weren’t going to say no to anything you asked.’ He was always kidding with me. I said, ‘If I’d have known that, I’d have asked for a lot more money!’”

Rutledge began his uphill battle of replacing the old blended Four Roses with Four Roses Bourbon throughout the country starting close to home.

“We started Four Roses in Kentucky,” he recalls. “If we can’t be successful in our home of Kentucky, how can we be a success in California or New York any, anywhere in between?”

Over the next 11 years, Rutledge pounded the pavement bringing the story of Four Roses to bartenders, whiskey fans, and anyone who would listen. His work helped to usher in a golden era not only for the Four Roses brand but also for Kentucky bourbon as a whole, often appearing alongside other legendary bourbon distillers like Jimmy Russell and Booker Noe.

Retirement Doesn’t Always Mean Retirement

In 2015 Rutledge retired from Four Roses. Kirin wanted him off the production floor and on the road full time in an emeritus role with no meaningful tie to the distillery’s operations. But he wanted to continue his work as a distiller, so after leaving he quickly got back into the game. By February 2016 he had the opportunity to work on a project at Castle & Key for a Louisville philanthropist.

“I always told people I’d like to end my life leaning over a fermenter, checking the quality, smelling it, tasting it, you know, putting my finger in and getting too big a whiff of CO2 and it’s all over, you know, my life, career, and everything,” he laughs.

In addition to staying on the production side, Rutledge continued building his legacy by mentoring others. Dixon Dedman, founder of Kentucky-based 2XO Whiskey, has long looked up to Rutledge, and still calls on him for blending advice.

“We talked through the philosophy of blending and how things work, why things work, why things don’t work, and the mystery of why some things that should work don’t work,” Dedman says. “I consider him a mentor, my mentor. We had a connection, but he didn’t need to share the time, share the knowledge, share the wisdom with me that he did. I am eternally and forever grateful for that because he just really helped me figure a lot of things out.”

And that is a story that echoes across the industry. Rutledge is the kind of person who will always answer the phone — gatekeeping is not in his vocabulary.

In 2021, Pennyroyal Distillery co-founder Ross Hutchison began helping some friends build a distillery in Adair County, Ky. Eventually Rutledge visited the site and agreed to work with the company, which began by sourcing barrels of whiskey. Fortunately there were plenty of barrels available that Rutledge had distilled at Castle & Key that had reached maturity, so Echoes of Oak was born.

“I remember sitting in his truck and riding over there, and he was telling me some stories as if I didn’t know who he was,” Hutchison says. “I absolutely knew who he was and how important he was. But Jim just kind of nonchalantly will mention things and talk about various people he’s met or things he’s done in a casual way, not a boasting way.”

Rutledge is showing no signs of slowing down. He’s working where he can, lamenting the downturn of the distilling industry. But he says that if things turn around he’d love to be back in a distillery making whiskey again, a sentiment he says is echoing through all of the distilleries with paused production right now.

“No matter where I worked, there’s a lot of hard jobs, a lot of heartaches sometimes, but I love the industry,” Rutledge says. “And I’ll go as long as I can, as long as I have something to do. I hope I don’t run out of things to do.”

content:
Cheap bourbon isn’t glamorous. The labels don’t tout special barrel finishes or unique age statements. The bottles won’t sit on the back of your home bar gathering the dust that will only be wiped off when a special occasion compels you to do so.

A reliable bottle of cheap bourbon makes up for these perceived deficiencies in numerous ways. It can provide the backbone for an Old Fashioned, a Boulevardier, or any bourbon cocktail that tickles your fancy. It can become the juice you reach for for a nighttime tipple before heading off to bed. It can also be an easy bottle to share with friends during a casual gathering. At a time when the phrase “in this economy?” can be said unironically, having a solid, cost-effective bourbon at the ready feels more important than ever.

Because of their price tags, cheap bourbons don’t always get the love they should compared to the Pappys and Wellers of the world. As such, there are plenty of wallet-friendly labels that coast under the radar as underrated gems. But which ones in this unique category deserve a little more attention? We asked 13 bartenders to find out. Here’s what they had to say.

The most underrated cheap bourbon, according to bartenders:

  • Four Roses Yellow Label
  • Old Bardstown 90 Proof
  • Old Grand-Dad Bonded
  • Woodford Reserve Kentucky Straight Bourbon
  • Woodford Reserve Wheated Bourbon
  • Great Jones Bourbon
  • Wild Turkey 101
  • Basil Hayden
  • Michter’s US*1 Bourbon
  • Old Grand-Dad 114
  • Brother’s Bond
  • Old Forester 100
  • Knob Creek 9-Year-Old Small Batch

“I think my favorite value bourbon is Four Roses Yellow Label. You can find it for about $30 at your nearest liquor store. It’s spicy, has that astringent mid-palate you’re looking for, and a lovely dried fruit finish. It’s not overproof, but has enough character to make it a solid choice for cocktailing, and a shot of it goes wonderfully with your favorite beer.” —Lucky Preksto, bar director, Bufón, New York City

“Old Bardstown 90 Proof. Produced by the Willett Distillery, and made from their own distillate — in other words, not sourced — for the last decade or so. This bottle delivers Willett quality at a wallet-friendly price. We keep it in the well at both of our venues, and it’s great in classic whiskey cocktails. It’s a great bottle to feature, especially if you’re building out a bar program that leans heavily on independent producers.” —Scott Stroemer, beverage director, Galit and Cafe Yaya, Chicago

“The best underrated bourbon under $35 is Old Grand-Dad Bonded. It has the proof, it has the age, it has the history. Having a high-rye mash bill means it is spicy enough to be seen in a cocktail, while the corn provides the delicate kiss needed for sipping neat. More importantly; it makes me feel good and nostalgic. This [label] was enjoyed by many others before me; knowing that I share a connection with someone long ago, whom I have never met, makes it all the better.” —Zack Atzert, head bartender, The Fountain Inn, Washington, D.C.

“Without a doubt, the best affordable daily bourbon to me is Woodford Reserve Kentucky Straight Bourbon. It’s handsome enough to proudly display on the counter, smooth enough to sip neat, and robust enough to stand up in a classic cocktail. Although some might argue about it being a cheap bourbon, you can still find Woodford for around $30 at one of the big box liquor stores. If you want an underrated variation on this classic, you can always try the Woodford Reserve Wheated Bourbon.” —Timofei Osipenko, bar director, Bar Iris, San Francisco

“One of my favorite parts of being in hospitality is introducing someone to something they weren’t expecting to love. Great Jones is one of those bottles for me. Smooth, rich, and just a little spicy, with vanilla, caramel, and toasted oak, it’s dangerously easy to like. If you’re a bourbon lover, you’ll appreciate it. If you think you’re not a bourbon person? That’s even better — let me pour you one and see what you think. And I love that it’s a New York bourbon — sipping it here at our bar surrounded by Hudson County history just feels right. Skip the hyped bottles and try something unexpected like Great Jones. You might just find your new favorite bourbon.” —Weng Lee, general manager, Halifax and Living Room Bar, Hoboken, N.J.

“Wild Turkey 101. It is usually under $35 and offers a lot of flavor for the price. It has a nice balance of caramel, vanilla, oak, and spice, with enough character to enjoy neat or in a cocktail. I especially like it in an Old Fashioned because the higher proof gives the drink more flavor without needing a lot of ingredients. It is also a great option for people who want a quality bourbon without spending too much. It is an easy bottle to keep at home, considering the price.” —Kelly Duong, general manager and mixologist, Kyojin, Washington, D.C.

“For me, this comes in two parts. Old Grand-Dad is the go-to whenever my friends and I go out and want a round of quick and affordable — but potent — shots. Far from subtle, this bourbon delivers a bold, robust character with a punch of spice that practically demands you clear your airway before taking the shot. Its high-rye mash bill stands front and center, coating the palate in a rich, peppery heat that really commands attention. On the flip side, you have Basil Hayden. It’s crafted at the same distillery as Old Grand-Dad and utilizes nearly the same mash bill. Yet a distinct distillation approach produces a far lighter, smoother, and more approachable spirit marked by gentler baking spices infused with sweet vanilla notes. It’s what to reach for when you prefer a smooth, easy-sipping pour to unwind.” —Justin Young, lead bartender, Farm Bar Lakeview, Chicago

“Michter’s US*1 Bourbon offers really good value for the quality of their whiskey. What I appreciate about Michter’s is the attention they give to the production process. The brand traces its history back to a Pennsylvania whiskey operation founded in 1753, and today there is still a strong focus on how the whiskey is made rather than simply on having a fancy label.” —José Maria Dondé Rangel, beverage director, The Bedford and Mexi, NYC

“It’s a toss-up, but I’d go with either Wild Turkey 101 and Old Grand-Dad 114. Both feel like steals for their price point and can usually be found for under $35. Wild Turkey 101 delivers classic bourbon flavors with rich caramel, vanilla, and spice, making it a great pour whether you choose to serve it neat or in cocktails. Old Grand-Dad 114 has a higher-proof punch and a rye-forward profile that gives you tastes of spice, oak, and sweetness that are rare for its price range. These two bottles remain some of the best values in bourbon for bartenders, and it’s hard to beat either one when it comes to quality, consistency, and affordability.” —Tony Rice, director of operations, Il Cervo, Milwaukee

“Four Roses Bourbon has always been my easy choice, starting back in its ‘Yellow Label’ days. Light on the spicy notes with a little citrus and subtle fruit, but still maintaining its structure. It works well in any whiskey-based cocktail but has enough complexity to sip on its own. It is also the go-to at my local bars for cocktails, sips, and celebrations!” —Michael Vollmer, director of beverage and programming, InterContinental San Diego, San Diego

“I would suggest Brother’s Bond Kentucky Straight Bourbon. While it was created by actors Ian Somerhalder and Paul Wesley, many people are surprised to discover that this small-batch bourbon is far more than a celebrity-backed label. It delivers a smooth, balanced profile with rich notes of caramel, vanilla, and oak, making it equally enjoyable neat or in a well-crafted cocktail. This is my go-to sipping bourbon; the craftsmanship and quality shine through in every sip, offering an approachable yet complex bourbon experience.” —Amanda Walsh, director of food and beverage, Ma Streeter’s Bourbon Lounge, Chicago

“While I have many favorites in this category behind the bar, I frequently default to Old Forester 100. It has the versatility to be mixed in cocktails and poured as a sipper, which I feel is something few and far between at this price point. Its robust profile and flavor complexity also easily outperforms its modest price tag. It has a distinct brown sugar, caramelized banana quality, and with the spirit sitting at 100 proof, it’s a perfect choice inside of many classic whiskey cocktails. In addition, the spirit rounds out nicely with bold oak and a nutty finish, giving it the ability to be enjoyed neat or over a large cube!” —Tanner Scott, food and beverage director, Skaneateles Fields Resort & Spa, Skaneateles, N.Y.

“Knob Creek 9 Year Old Small Batch gets missed or dismissed by some, but it is a bourbon that should be on everyone’s short list, especially if that list is short on cash. Knob Creek 9 Year is a great bourbon to start a cocktail or a mixed drink. Hailing from the Jim Beam family, you’ll find rich caramel notes, slightly nutty tones and the faintest oak lingering on your palate. Old Fashioneds are a must-try with Knob Creek, and so are Bourbon Manhattans. You can also put this bourbon in a sour and you will not be disappointed, or have a highball for a refreshing after-work treat. Knob Creek 9 Year is 100 proof, so it may not be your first choice as a sipper. But as an aged bourbon, it will definitely add to the rotation on your home back bar. And for under $35, it’s not to be overlooked.” —Andrea Johns, beverage manager, AYLA, Houston

content:
Chardonnay has long been one of the world’s most popular wine grapes. Though it originated in Burgundy, the variety is now grown across every major wine region, and as it spread, many different vinification styles emerged. Despite its versatility, Chardonnay became synonymous with the heavily oaked, buttery style from California that dominated the market in the 1990s, resulting in the “Anything but Chardonnay” movement of drinkers set on avoiding the grape at all costs for fear of its intensely oaky flavors.

And while a new wave of Chardonnay is staking its claim among winemakers — one that heralds the grape’s brighter, fresher qualities — there are still many producers embracing its rich, oaky side. But it’s all about balance. While the wines that gave Chardonnay a bad rap lean too heavy into that big, buttery mouthfeel, there are some producers that nail the tension between bright fruit, crisp acidity, and oak influence.

We rounded up the best Chardonnays that display that classic oak character, without totally overwhelming the palate. We steered clear of butter-bombs, opting instead for those that walk the line between heft and elegance. For those looking to embrace Chardonnay’s silkier side, here are the best oaky, buttery Chardonnays.

Concannon Vineyard Reserve Chardonnay 2024

As one of the oldest family wineries in the Livermore Valley, Concannon has mastered the grapes that thrive on California’s Central Coast — one of which is Chardonnay. The palate is rich and buttery, but brought to life by tinges of bright fruit. In structure just as in flavor, Concannon strikes that balance: Though it clocks in at 14.1 percent, which is on the heftier end for the grape, the Reserve Chardonnay delivers a salivating acidity that brightens the ensemble all up.

Rombauer Carneros Chardonnay 2024

Rombauer is one of the pioneers of big, bold American Chardonnay, and the 2024 Carneros bottling lives up to its reputation. The Carneros AVA offers a cool climate that lends an incredible brightness to the palate, complementing its otherwise silky, rich mouthfeel. Rounding out the wine are notes of vanilla, almond, and ripe apples.

Average price: $42
Rating: 94

See Review

Desforges Suzanne’s Block Chardonnay 2024

Desforges is a family-owned winery in Sonoma County that farms its own estate. Among its plots are specific parcels named after members of the family. This Chardonnay from co-founder Suzanne’s block hits markets on an occasional basis — only when Suzanne and other family members deem the vintage worthy enough to drink at their own dinner table. Aged in French oak from the Louis Latour Cooperage in Burgundy, this single-barrel expression opens with an aromatic nose of apples, lemon, and vanilla. On the palate, a rich mouthfeel melds with a gripping acidity.

Average price: $58
Rating: 93

See Review

Soter Vineyards Estates Chardonnay 2022

Soter Vineyards is part of a wave of Willamette winemakers ushering American Chardonnay into its next era — one that celebrates the tension between a classic buttery profile and bright acidity. Soter’s Estates Chardonnay is the quintessence of this new-school style: It combines notes of bistro butter, oyster brine, herbs, and ripe fruit. All the while, a refreshing, almost salty acidity buttons this expression up.

Average price: $60
Rating: 96

See Review

Domaine Serene ‘Evenstad Reserve’ Chardonnay 2023

To make its Evenstad Reserve bottling, Domaine Serene identifies and blends the best barrels of Chardonnay from its cellar. The juice, sourced from the Willamette Valley’s Dundee Hills AVA, is aged for 13 months in a blend of new and used French oak, imparting a creamy texture and flavors of vanilla and salted butter. Cutting through that plush mouthfeel are notes of lemon curd and freshly cut grass.

Average price: $75
Rating: 97

See Review

Garden Creek Estate Clonal Selection Chardonnay 2022

Situated in California’s Alexander Valley, Garden Creek works with a number of Chardonnay clones. For its Estate Clonal Selection bottling, the winery first fermented six clones in individual French oak barrels before blending. On the nose, this Chardonnay is a bit of a red herring: Its creamy yet savory aromas suggest it’ll be a total butter-bomb, but the palate is much more balanced, adding acidity, crisp citrus fruit, and herbs to the mix.

Rating: 96

St. Innocent Winery Enchanted Way Vineyard Triangle Block Chardonnay 2023

St. Innocent from Oregon’s Willamette Valley is lauded for its Pinot Noir, but it produces just-as stellar expressions of the red grape’s counterpart, Chardonnay. Coming from its high-altitude Enchanted Way vineyard, this Chardonnay — made with just a touch of new French oak — opens with stone fruit and citrus zest on the nose. The lingering palate brings notes of creamy lemon curd.

content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. It was a quiet week on the news front, but as we gear up for gifting season, there are a ton of new product drops. We have updates on Southern Glazer’s bribery snafu, OpenTable’s 2026 restaurant report, and the latest releases.

News to know:

  • California state officials step in on Southern’s bribery scandal: After Southern Glazer’s entered a non-prosecution agreement and paid $12.5 million to settle its yearslong bribery case with the Department of Justice and the Alcohol and Tobacco Trade Bureau, California state regulators are now pursuing their own investigation on the nation’s largest alcohol distributor. A state official told the San Francisco Chronicle that it intends to determine whether the distributor’s wrongdoings caused harm to small retailers and consumers.
  • Average spend at restaurants rises: According to this year’s OpenTable Restaurant Impact Report, the average per-person restaurant spend was $60 in the last 12 months, up 3 percent year-over-year. The report also found that the food service industry is slated to reach $1.55 billion in total sales for 2026, which would mark a nearly 5 percent jump from last year.
  • Carlsberg intends to close an English brewery: The U.K. subsidiary of Carlsberg announced its plans to close Marton’s Brewery in Burton on Trent next summer. The termination is expected to affect over 300 workers. Production for some of the brands such as Hobgoblin and McEwan’s will shift elsewhere and remain in the Carlsberg portfolio, whereas the company plans on shopping around other brands currently under its purview.

Product releases to watch:

summary:

Though the drink’s appeal is timeless, Guinness is experiencing a heyday among contemporary drinkers. content:
To some, there’s no better drink than a perfect pint of Guinness. Fans of the Irish stout prize the beer for its creamy texture, toasty flavors, and stately appearance. Though the drink’s appeal is timeless, Guinness is experiencing a heyday among contemporary drinkers. And with that bump in popularity comes a surge of fads, with trends like “splitting the G,” 60/40 pours, and Turbo Guinnesses swarming pubs and social media feeds.

While tinkering with the perfection of a meticulous two-part pour may seem sacrilegious — and is sure to spur on intense debate — the practice can actually be traced back centuries. In the 1700s, it became common in English pubs to mix dark stouts with a pale ale or lager as a sort-of beer cocktail to personalize the drink to customers’ palates.

The trend stuck, and eventually, mixing Guinness with pale beers became known as the Black and Tan, which the Oxford English Dictionary suggests was first recorded in 1889 — though it’s now commonly referred to by a different name. Guinness’ marketing later made deliberate efforts in normalizing mixing the beverage into cocktails.

Since then, a suite of Guinness combos have emerged — ranging from classic mixtures with other iconic beers to unexpected marriages with bright green energy drinks. Here are eight Guinness combos to try to zhuzh up your pint.

Blacksmith

The Blacksmith brings together two Irish pub staples, mixing Guinness with Smithwicks. The Irish Red Ale is made with caramel malts, introducing a toffee-like flavor profile. The Smithwicks addition complements Guinness’ toasty notes while adding a fruit-forward, crisp edge to the typically creamy pint.

Black and Blue

A somewhat less conventional pairing, the Black and Blue is a mixture of Guinness and Blue Moon. The U.S.-produced Belgian-style wheat beer offers radically different flavors than Guinness, with notes of juicy citrus and savory spice. But similar to the Smithwick’s in the Blacksmith, the Blue Moon brings a fruity brightness to Guinness. Garnish it with an orange wheel to amp up the citrus.

Black Velvet

Unlike the Guinness-and-other-beer combos that dominate this list, the Black Velvet merges the stout with sparkling wine, typically Champagne. It also is the only combo to switch up the format, opting for a flute rather than the standard pint glass. The bubbles from the wine accentuate those in the nitro stout, and the Champagne’s creamier notes also help to emphasize the Guinness’ rich texture, coming together in a velvety sip.

Black Castle

While many classic Guinness combos counterbalance the dark stout with a light and fruity beverage, the Black Castle doubles down on its roasted malt notes. Mixing Guinness with the U.K.-brewed Newcastle Brown Ale, the Black Castle celebrates both beers’ nutty, caramel, and chocolatey notes.

Guinness and Black

Also known as a Black and Black, a Guinness and Black is just the traditional pint with a dash of blackcurrant cordial. The syrupy cordial mellows out the stout’s rougher edges, and imparts a fruity kick instead. Its flavor profile is at once breakfast- and dessert-like, marrying warm, chocolatey notes with dark fruited undertones.

Black and Gold

A Black and Gold is equal-parts hard cider and Guinness, a combo that is also referred to as a Snakebite. To achieve the signature look, a half-pint of Guinness is carefully pulled above cider or ale to not mix the two, but rather layer the less-dense stout atop. The result is a striking contrast between the dark Guinness and golden cider at the bottom.

Half and Half

A Half and Half is made by layering a half pint of Guinness over a pale ale or lager, most commonly Guinness-owned Harp. The resulting combination dilutes Guinness’ toasted malt flavors with Harp’s crisper, wheatier profile. This is considered the modern iteration of the now-retired Black and Tan.

Gonster

Many of the mixtures on this list are pub classics, but the recent surge in Guinness’ popularity has spurred some drinkers to come up with chaotic — err, experimental — combos. Also known as the “Billie Irish,” the Gonster layers Guinness over the electric green Monster Energy Nitro. It first delivers the familiar flavors of Guinness before a surge of sugary citric acid comes through. Approach with caution.

content:
Set your navigation southwest from Paris and follow your wine-loving heart to the Loire. There, along the curving river’s central stretch, you’ll find the country’s third-largest wine region: a verdant, chateau-studded valley where waves of vines give birth to grapes destined for an effervescent future.

You’ll find it in a bottle of Bouvet-Ladubay’s sparkling wine.

Bouvet-Ladubay is located in Saumur, a Loire region that is one of France’s most acclaimed for its sparkling wines, and since the mid-19th century, that’s been Bouvet’s specialty. Founded by husband and wife Etienne Bouvet and Célestine Ladubay in 1851, and taken over by the Monmousseau family after the former’s death in 1908, the maison has since grown into the largest producer of méthode traditionnelle sparkling wine in Saumur. 

This year, Bouvet celebrates 175 years, and there’s no time like an anniversary to pop open a bottle of bubbly while learning more about the praised French producer and the true lure of the Loire. 

Sparkling wine is the sign of a good time: shimmering on a sunny seaside terrace; glowing under candlelight at a corner bistro; reflecting the dancing lights of a disco ball in a glass. It’s a beverage that’s synonymous with luxury and celebration, but that doesn’t mean you should wait for a specific moment to open a bottle. Bouvet-Ladubay crafts traditional wines for modern times. Think of their sparkling wines as the perfect accompaniment for all occasions. 

The Signature Limestone At the Heart of the Loire

Before diving into the Bouvet bouquet, it’s important to understand the history and geology of the Loire Valley, a UNESCO World Heritage site (acknowledged in 2000 for its “outstanding cultural landscape”) where architecture, agriculture and the region’s wines are all defined by a unique local limestone known as tuffeau.

Underfoot is where the magic happens, the natural sorcery responsible for the health and flavor of the fruit at the heart of the Loire. A soft, porous stone, tuffeau is the key component of Saumur’s signature chalky soil, fostering a friendly growing environment for the region’s grapes. 

On the taste and texture front, tuffeau is also to credit for the pleasant minerality you’ll find in many of the region’s wines. (For example, in a bottle of Bouvet Signature Brut.)

Above-ground, the limestone has long played a part in the life and look of the Loire. An almost-luminescent rock, the “stone of light” was the building material of choice for the rich, the royal and the religious. And it was limestone’s harvesting that, centuries later, would create the very setting for Bouvet-Ladubay today.

Subterranean Sipping: the Cellars of Bouvet-Ladubay

Cave à vin is French for wine cellar, and you can take the word “cave” quite literally in the Loire.

When the harvesting of limestone began in the 11th century, Saint Florent monks hollowed out some of the hillside, digging deep into the earth to acquire the stone to build their abbey. In the 19th century, some of the quarries left behind were transformed into wine cellars, sacred spaces where one can now commune with a slightly different kind of divine.

When Bouvet-Ladubay was founded 175 years ago, its cellars were built beneath the remains of an old abbey. There the limestone also does the crucial work of natural climate control to elegantly mature the wines. 

Today, a visit to Bouvet-Ladubay includes the opportunity to roam through eight kilometers of cellars where their wines are stored and aged. In this enchanting underground location in the Loire, thousands of visitors pass through the cellars each year (on foot or by bike), then sip sparkling wines in the adjacent tasting room.

The Beauty of the Blend: A Tale of Three Grapes

In the (translated) words of Bouvet-Ladubay’s Patrice Monmousseau: “Nothing is more essential to the finesse of bubbles than art and artists.” And whether you consider it more of an art or a science, Cuvée is about the beauty of the blend.

A product of countless hands and hearts, Bouvet-Ladubay works with around 80 winegrowers on more than 100 different plots, and their wines are made from three grapes that thrive within the Loire’s special soil: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, and Cabernet Franc. 

Chenin Blanc is the Loire’s signature grape, a variety with fruity aromas up front and a balanced palate that grows richer over time. Chardonnay is newer to the Saumur region since the 20th century, but has found a happy home in its limestone soils, resulting in firm, full-bodied and truly fine white wines. Making its Loire debut in the 11th century, Cabernet Franc (used in rosé) is the first red grape variety to arrive in the region, and is characterized by aromas of ripe, dark fruit, subtle spice notes, and a deep ruby hue. 

It’s from these grapes that the year’s Cuvée is created: a bouquet that acts as a sippable time capsule and a testament to today’s terroir. Carefully and expertly orchestrated, it’s blended by Bouvet-Ladubay to ensure sparkling wine excellence. It’s the benchmark the producer has prided itself on since the very beginning. 

A Global Legacy: 175 Years of Wine and Culture 

With Juliette Monmousseau at the helm of Bouvet, bubbles remain a family business fueled by four generations of pride and passion. These are qualities that extend far past France’s borders and beyond the world of winemaking.

Following an “Appointment of the House of Lords,” Etienne Bouvet was named the official supplier to the British Parliament back in the 1870s, and today Bouvet’s wines are now exported to around 50 countries (including the United States through Kobrand). And while wine making is an art, it’s not the only expression Bouvet is focused on. The brand has also long been synonymous with culture, and in the 1990s, the Monmousseaus opened the Bouvet Ladubay Contemporary Art Center to revive the tradition of artistic patronage in the Loire. They also restored and reopened the theatre that had originally been built by Bouvet.

Easy Elegance: a Taste of the Good Life For All

Offering elegance and ease, the Bouvet Crémant de Loire is sippable all meal long and, with notes of green apple and toast, pairs particularly well with poultry and freshwater fish. The Bouvet Rosé Excellence is perfect for popping at a summer picnic, its pink fizz serving as a fresh, slightly fruity foil for spicy, saucy barbeque. And with white-gold bubbles and notes of brioche and pear, the Bouvet Signature Brut is an effervescent accompaniment to richer meals or pairs perfectly with simpler dishes such as a cheese plate.

It’s not just a matter of the vintages’ versatility but also their value. Bouvet-Ladubay prides itself on accessible elegance. Merging quality with affordability, these sparklings offer an authentic taste of the Loire — and of the good life — for all who open a bottle.

content:
Over decades of regular trips to Europe, Regine Rousseau, the Chicago-based founder of wine marketing and events consultancy Shall We Wine, never really subscribed to the directive often preached by U.S. travel publications: When traveling abroad, try not to let your American show.

“Number one: I like wearing really bright colors, so I rarely blend in anywhere,” says Rousseau, also senior sales advisor at Verve Wine Chicago. “Number two, I am Black, and typically when I’m traveling, I am one of few Black people, even in the places I visit in Europe. So typically they look at me and know I’m American.”

Having known what it is to be othered, this Haitian-American prefers to understand a bit of the culture she’s in rather than insert herself. With time and miles, she’s learned she’d prefer lingering over cramming in as many stops as possible. Though she’s a 70-30 wine-to-cocktail drinker, she often lets her curiosity and the environment lead her drinking choices. Thus, as a first timer in bars in Portugal and Ischia, she probably asked the bartender, “What’s your specialty?” or “What is it you make that no one else makes better than you?”

“When I’m traveling, I want to sit, I want to think, I want to have a conversation, and I really want the place to become part of me and hopefully leave something in the place I’m visiting,” Rousseau says.

Her words exude the sensibility of a seasoned traveler: One doesn’t have to fake blending in to be a good visitor.

Historically, the American Tourist has conjured some silly, occasionally unfortunate tropes: shouty, bald-faced enthusiasm through the lens of American exceptionalism. Fanny packs crammed with cash tips deposited in excess regardless of local customs. Athleisure! A penchant for vodka and ice, not to mention the trails of takeaway coffee cups we leave in our wake. We’re boisterous and opinionated, occasionally overly friendly. This shows up in our drinking behavior, too — the way we demand our Martinis just so and willingly chat up strangers at the bar. Occasionally, our exceptionalism crops up in our very American cocktail requests (Skinny Bitch, anyone?).

But with experience — nowadays Americans globetrot much more — there seems to be promise that the American tourist will embrace more of the local and the unfamiliar. Or, at least, fake it convincingly enough.

The Tenacious Martini Tourist

Over the past decade, international travel among U.S. tourists surged roughly 71 percent, per data from the International Trade Administration. In 2025, Americans took a record 24 million trips to Europe, a number that’s expected to climb by another 5 percent by the end of this year, according to The Wall Street Journal. Does all that extra mileage translate to shedding certain stereotypes as Americans descend on the drinking establishments of Madrid, London, and Rome? European bartenders say the thread connecting U.S. travelers in 2026 is largely one of curiosity and openness … though we still love our vodka.

“What can I say? Americans at the bar are entertaining, in a positive way,” says Giorgio Bargiani, assistant director of mixology at The Connaught Bar in London. Maybe he has to say that; after all, North Americans are the majority demographic at this luxury cocktail bar and its iconic namesake hotel. Bargiani can pick out U.S. visitors right away by how they engage staff and fellow customers.

“It starts when they arrive at the bar and you treat them as everybody else,” he says, “but straight away there’s conversation. There’s no shyness. There is always interest that, in my eyes, feels genuine, compared to other cultures where this interest is not necessarily false, but more polite than genuine.”

The interactions tend to spread beyond customer and bartender, until the whole bar seems to percolate with chatter about what everyone ordered and whether they like it. Of course, with gabby confidence comes opinions, of which Americans seem to proffer many, and often, about what’s in the glass. At Connaught Bar this holds especially true for Martinis, which are its bread and butter, to the tune of 30,000 made each year.

“When I moved to London [in 2014], I could see the average American guest coming in with a very precise idea of how they like their Martinis, for instance —” most notably with vodka over gin.

The same goes for ordering Martinis garnished with blue cheese-stuffed olives, as U.S. customers have been known to ask of Arturo Burzio, head mixologist at the luxury Madrid hotel Rosewood Villa Magna. (Hey, Northern Spain makes great blue cheese, right?)

“Every time you land somewhere in Italy, someone says, ‘let’s have a Spritz.’ It’s like, why? Of course, I’ll do it out of love and to participate.”

The complaint that a good Martini is hard to find is a common refrain among Americans in Europe. No matter that across much of the E.U., a “cocktail” more often refers to “something fruity, sweet, and sour” — we seem determined to believe that the savory, boozy, very American drink is a widely shared cultural touchstone.

Chalk it up to the glut of choice that pervades consumerist American culture, but we also seem to love customizing even the most classic cocktails. That the traditional Margarita contains no added sugar doesn’t stop U.S. customers requesting the cocktail be made “without sugar,” nodding to the sweeter versions commonplace around the U.S., Burzio says. He is likewise accustomed to fielding American requests for U.S. spirit substitutions, like bourbon and specific vodka brands, plus the occasional ask for American-born concoctions, like the Cosmopolitan, Vodka Cranberry, and, regrettably, the aforementioned Skinny Bitch — made with vodka, lime juice, and soda water.

You Can Take the Tourist out of America…

You can’t always take the American out of the tourist. Even the well-traveled among us occasionally give ourselves away by ordering exactly what we want, regardless of the place or its legendary status.

The historic, recently reopened cafe, cocktail bar and restaurant Bar della Pace, a stone’s throw from Rome’s Piazza Navona, is best known for spritzes, Bellinis, and Rossinis served with a side of potato chips and people watching. Some American visitors happily comply with ordering these customary aperitivi; but just as many may request a Martini or Espresso Martini, per director and manager Maria Iemma.

“They’re always friendly, cheerful and respectful,” Iemma says, wryly adding, it helps that they tip so generously.

By comparison, old hand U.S. travelers are more comfortable exploring unfamiliar ingredients and local spirits. “They may ask for recommendations, describe the flavors they enjoy, and let the bartender guide them,” Burzio notes.

They even come around to gin Martinis, Bargiani says, “because when in London, we drink gin Martinis.”

Rousseau has markedly evolved in how she travels since she first visited France as a senior in college and was horrified to learn that “cooked” steak could still be bloody inside. Most notably, she says, she’s become more of a participant than a consumer of other cultures. After all, the joy of rituals lies in experiencing them as intended.

She still recalls sitting at a bar in Porto on her first trip to Portugal and asking the bartender, “What’s interesting that is truly Porto?” Then boom! Out came that honeyed, low-ABV white port and tonic, “and it was Porto.” She drinks them whenever she is back in Portugal’s second-largest city.

She could, however, do without the sugared, sunset-colored Aperol Spritz altogether, though she can’t seem to escape it.

“Every time you land somewhere in Italy, someone says, ‘let’s have a Spritz.’ It’s like, why? Of course, I’ll do it out of love and to participate.”

When in Rome, right?

Drink the place. It’s a simple mantra that bears repeating, as our shrinking globe brings more of the world to our fingertips without the benefit of context. If Warren Johnson, the well-traveled partner at Saint Urban’s in Charleston, S.C., had stuck with his preferred beverage order of wine while visiting Antwerp, Belgium, this summer, he might have missed out on Westmalle Dubbel, the iconic reddish-brown ale made by Trappist monks just north of the city. Fortunately, he followed the local advice, and changed just a little in the process.

“Its complex, deeply bitter, fruity, and herbaceous notes seriously hit the mark,” Johnson recalls, “and with that, I’m now a beer drinker.”

content:
Gin was somewhat of a tough sell in the early days of the craft cocktail revival. Consumers were more reluctant to dive into the botanical booze like they had for brown spirits. This sometimes compelled bartenders who embraced gin to hatch creative ways to promote the category. In one legendary story, for instance, a member of Pegu Club’s roster of acclaimed bartenders would sell guests on gin by telling them it was juniper-flavored vodka.

A couple of decades later, and the gin category has blossomed into a fascinating space that virtually demands exploration from the spirits enthusiast. This is partially due to an abundance of expressions from around the world, many of which create innovative ways to build flavor around gin’s required juniper berries.

The level of choice can admittedly cause analysis paralysis among gin newcomers. Finding the right bottle to kick off a personal gin journey can be tough. Having a trusted guide that understands gin can reduce some of the difficulty, and there may not be a better font of knowledge to draw from than a bar professional. With that in mind, we asked 15 bartenders to highlight their choice for the gin that’s perfect for beginners.

Best gin for beginners, according to bartenders:

  • Bayab Orange and Marula Gin
  • Citadelle Gin
  • Fords Gin
  • Aria Classic Dry Gin
  • Condesa Gin ‘Clásica’
  • Bluecoat American Dry Gin
  • Suntory Roku Gin
  • Beefeater London Dry Gin
  • Hendrick’s Gin
  • Bayab Palm & Pineapple
  • Drumshanbo Gunpowder Gin
  • Tanqueray
  • Letherbee Gin
  • Nolet’s Silver Dry Gin
  • The Botanist Islay Dry Gin

“Bayab Orange and Marula gin distilled in South Africa is an excellent introduction for those that may find gin to be medicinal in flavor. Marula is a sub-Saharan fruit that truly represents the place where it grows: bright, vibrant, and intense. This helps allow the gin to make a great dry Martini and a great Gimlet; which is not always the case. Having the juniper and spice play a more minor role than the citrus is what sets this gin apart from the rest.” —Zack Atzert, head bartender, The Fountain Inn, Washington, D.C.

“For something right down the middle, I would go with Citadelle Gin. It’s a very approachable London style gin. It’s super easy-drinking with a wonderful punchy juniper that isn’t overpowering. They are also one of the only global gin brands to harvest and cultivate their own juniper, so they have very fresh botanicals.” —Jarett Karlsberg, beverage director, Wythe Hotel, Brooklyn

“Fords Gin is approachable for beginners because it’s balanced rather than juniper-heavy, so it doesn’t hit you with that ‘pine tree’ intensity some gins have. It was developed with input from bartenders to be versatile, meaning it works well in almost any classic cocktail. This makes it a good all-purpose bottle to learn how to make gin-based drinks. It’s also reasonably priced and widely available, so it’s an easy, low-risk way to start exploring gin.” —Charlotte Marshall, beverage director, Nic & Junior’s Tavern, Chicago

“A strong, juniper-forward flavor may not be what beginners are looking for. With that in mind, Aria Classic Dry Gin strikes a beautiful balance between the traditional London Dry style and approachable floral and citrus notes. It has layers of flavor that stand alone well in a dry Martini but also integrate perfectly into any classic gin cocktail. My summer go-to is an Aria Gin & Tonic, garnished with a fresh lime and a sprig of thyme. However, with winter right around the corner, I will soon be reaching for a classic Aria Negroni.” —Jessica Brown, bar director, Nostrana, Portland, Ore.

“One of my favorite gins for beginners, and in general, is Condesa Gin ‘Clásica.’ Condesa’s prioritization of Mexican botanicals over traditional ones found in London Dry gins such as palo santo and Mexican sage make it more palatable to someone new to gin, while making it softer on the palate. Its versatility is also a major plus; we love using it in White Negronis and Martinis alike.” —Ricky Dolinsky, beverage director, Dandelion and Keepers, New York City

“Bluecoat American Dry Gin is my no-brainer recommendation for anyone new to gin. Wonderfully textured and citrus-forward, it carries a subtle sweetness followed by a delicate, spicy finish. At 47 percent ABV, it’s dangerously sippable. From a practicality standpoint, Bluecoat is easygoing in a Martini, delightful in a Negroni, and resilient in just about any shaken cocktail.” —B. Cole, Head Bartender, Valerie, NYC

“Suntory Roku Gin is a great choice for anyone new to the world of gin. It’s expressive and approachable, showcasing delicate Japanese botanicals like sakura, yuzu, and sencha tea. Roku has significant floral and citrusy character without relying on the juniper-forward flavor that can be overwhelming for those new to drinking gin. It’s also a team player in cocktails, as its balanced profile blends harmoniously with other ingredients.” —Martha Davis, lead bartender, The Marigold Club, Houston

“Gin is a fantastic spirit. It comes in all shapes and sizes, so it is approachable for many different palates. For someone trying gin for the first time, I’d recommend a citrus-forward, London Dry style, and Beefeater London Dry Gin immediately comes to mind. It is crisp and clean, and true to its name, finishes dry. Also, If tonic is your mixer when you’re getting into gin, please make sure you’re using a great one. It matters.” —Sarah Clark, director of operations, The Dearborn, Chicago

“For someone new to gin, I would recommend Hendrick’s Gin. It is approachable without losing the character that makes gin unique. It has a smooth and easy-to-drink flavor, with light notes of cucumber and rose that make it less strong and traditional than some other gins. It also works well in simple cocktails like a Gin & Tonic, Martini, or Tom Collins. I think it is a good starting point because you can enjoy it on its own, but it also mixes well with different flavors.” —Kelly Duong, general manager and mixologist, Kyojin, Washington, D.C.

“For someone newer to gin, I think Bayab Palm & Pineapple is a really approachable entry point. The first thing you get is this bright, tropical pineapple character rather than being hit immediately with a ton of juniper. There’s still enough dryness, citrus, and botanical structure underneath it that it drinks like gin, but it gives you a familiar flavor to enter through. It’s a good example of how flavored gin can bring something very recognizable to a cocktail while still doing the job you need the gin to do.” —Kyle Jackson, beverage director, The Argyle, NYC

“I think people new to gin often have the misconception that it’s overly piney — like drinking a Christmas tree in a glass — or that it’s something their grandma drank. But there are plenty of gins that are much more approachable for beginners. Drumshanbo Gunpowder Gin, for example, is citrus- and tea-driven, with gentle spice notes that make it really enjoyable. For something even more familiar, Hendrick’s leans into cucumber and rose, creating a softer, more approachable profile. Both are great introductions to gin because they showcase its versatility without overwhelming someone who may not be accustomed to its distinctive botanicals.” —Daniel Navarro, lead bartender, CHICA, Las Vegas

“Starting off with a classic London Dry gin like Beefeater or Tanqueray is a great way to understand the category. These are classic styles where you can clearly identify the botanicals, especially juniper, along with citrus, coriander and other herbs and spices. Once you understand that classic profile, you can move into Japanese, Italian, Mexican, or small-distillery gins that use botanicals and ingredients that represent where they come from.” —José Maria Dondé Rangel, beverage director, The Bedford and Mexi, NYC

“Letherbee Gin is a versatile choice, ideal for beginners looking to craft a wide variety of cocktails. Because Letherbee does not chill-filter its gin, it retains all the rich essential oils extracted from botanicals like juniper, citrus, and aniseed. When mixed with water or other liquids, these oils bloom and create a distinct cloudy appearance, releasing an intense aroma that elevates classics like the Gin Martini or Gimlet. Additionally, Letherbee’s high proof, robust spice profile, and citrus notes allow it to complement citrus-forward drinks without being overshadowed by sugar or acid. This makes it an exceptional base for sour-style cocktails such as the Bee’s Knees, Gimlet, or Last Word. Really, it’s a great all-around gin for any bar.” —Andrew Thompson, beverage manager, Dicey’s Pizza &Tavern, Chicago

“For someone just getting into gin, I always recommend Nolet’s Silver Dry Gin because it’s beautifully floral and fruit-forward, with notes of rose, peach, and raspberry that make it softer and more approachable. I personally love it in a Gimlet because it’s bright, refreshing, dangerously crushable, and really showcases the beautiful complexity that a gin can possess.” —Jennifer Yim, master mixologist, Bellagio, Las Vegas

“To me, the classic starter gin is going to be a London dry gin. But if you want to go for a more botanical, citrusy forward gin, I would recommend The Botanist Islay Dry Gin. This gin really pushes botanical flavors, but does so without any added flavors or additives. It also makes a great Gin & Tonic.” —Galen Maclennan, beverage and general manager, Ferguson’s Country, Brooklyn

content:
This month marks 60 years in the bourbon industry for distilling legend Jim Rutledge. His claim to fame is bringing Four Roses Bourbon back to the United States after decades of only being sold in Japan and other foreign markets, a move that has earned him a venerated place among whiskey geeks. But since retiring from Four Roses in 2015 he’s continued to build his legacy, helping to launch numerous brands including Cream of Kentucky and Echoes of Oak, the latter of which he distilled at Castle & Key Distillery.

Over the last six decades, Rutledge has seen everything from computers replacing handwritten ledgers to extreme changes in demand, enduring a number of booms and busts in the market. He’s credited with rescuing Four Roses Bourbon from certain oblivion, and even retirement couldn’t stop him from continuing to shape the distilled spirits landscape in the U.S. The unwavering passion Rutledge has for bourbon continues to reverberate through the industry. Even after a lifetime working in bourbon, Rutledge takes every opportunity to work closely with distilling and to share his experience with those coming up in the industry.

The Seagram’s Days

In 1966, Rutledge took a job at Seagram’s Calvert Distillery on 7th Street Rd. in Louisville. After graduating from the University of Louisville and working at Sears for two years, he’d landed two offers: one at tobacco manufacturer Phillip Morris, where one of the perks was that he could smoke all the free cigarettes he wanted at lunch, and another at Seagram’s.

“I didn’t want to take the first job that was offered,” Rutledge recalls. “I was hoping to find something a little more interesting, and hopefully a career.”

He worked in research and development then as a case goods shipping supervisor, and eventually as a bottling line planner. Though he started gaining some experience in distillery production, he’d often get called back to bottling during the holiday rush. Back in those days, he says operators would use pencil marks on the valves to control the optimal temperature and flow on the stills, something that is controlled by computers now.

“But I never really had enough time to learn the distillery business,” he says.

In November of 1977, shortly after managing the transition to palletization in the warehouses, he was transferred to New York.

An Unexpected ‘Promotion’

“[One day] I snuck out [of work] about 20 minutes early to go bowling,” he recalls. “The guard stopped me as I was walking out the gate. He said, ‘Jim, the plant superintendent wants to see you.’ I said, ’Oh my gosh, how did he know I was leaving early?’ And so I walked down to his office carrying my bowling ball and sat down.”

The superintendent told him he was getting promoted to chief industrial engineer in New York. While that would ordinarily be cause for celebration, Rutledge was wary of the move, reluctant to uproot his family. But back in those days, he says, it was take the job or take a hike, so he took the job.

“I went bowling, and I bowled the worst game I’d ever had in my life,” he laughs.

He couldn’t sleep that night, envisioning never seeing a park or a softball field ever again. What’s more, by the time he got to New York the job title was changed from chief industrial engineer to assistant manager of the budgets and standards department.

He spent 15 years in New York working for Seagram’s, all the while pining for the production floor. Finally, in 1990, his reviewer asked if he was serious about wanting to go back to production, sharing that he would be retiring in the next couple of years and was looking for someone to head up the Four Roses Distillery in Kentucky.

Two years later he was called to a meeting in Louisville. The topic: returning to Kentucky to get back into the production side.

The Four Roses Years

Rutledge spent his first two years back in Kentucky in Cox’s Creek, turning the tiny bottling operation into the massive warehousing and bottling facility it is today. In November of 1994, Rutledge was slated to shift his focus to the Four Roses Distillery in Lawrenceburg, but he received some troubling news from the higher-ups at Seagram’s.

“They told me the quality, what comes off the still before it goes into a barrel, was so bad and had been so bad for about three and a half years that if it didn’t improve by summer shutdown the second week of June 1995, they would have to fire everybody at the distillery.”

At that time Four Roses Bourbon was only sold in foreign markets. In 1959 the brand had shifted its focus to international consumers, mainly Japan. The product called Four Roses that was for sale in the U.S. was a blended whiskey made in both Indiana and Maryland, and it was widely regarded as a bottom shelf product.

“The guy I was replacing stayed on through the end of the year,” Rutledge recalls. “I got to know the distillery operations and the people, the atmosphere at the time was just very, very caustic.”

Knowing that the distillery had no option other than to improve the quality, Rutledge remembers subtly pushing the distillery floor to refine its process. “Once everybody left for the day, I’d go over and spend the next shift entirely with the distillery operators, listening and learning,” he says. “I couldn’t tell anybody that the distillery was going to be shut down if we didn’t turn the quality around. I just told them I believe in quality and we’ve got to improve”

He’d arrive each day around 7 a.m. to prepare for the morning shift to start at 8 a.m. He’d walk through the distillery at least three times a day, getting to know everyone from clerical to maintenance. He wanted to get a feel for how things worked, what wasn’t working, and where improvements could be made, and for him that meant starting with the people.

“I remember one of the guys saying, ‘You know, all you management guys say that, but none of you ever mean it.’ And I said, ‘You’ll see.’”

“One of the things that he told me was to go talk to the guy that’s been running the still for 20 years and see what you could learn,” says master blender Ashley Barnes, who worked with Rutledge at Four Roses and is now an industry consultant. “He was always ready to share his knowledge and teach me something, and willing to be patient and answer all my questions. I started working with Jim in 2014, and full circle is I’m getting to work with him again on Jacob Spears.”

Rutledge says there was a rigid structure to a union shop, so much so that if he walked into the distillery and a valve needed to be turned he could not turn it himself — he’d have to find someone in maintenance to do it. But that’s precisely why he felt he needed to learn the system so fully, because everyone’s success depended on it.

“That’s the kind of atmosphere I’ve always believed in, working together. I felt like they might report to me, but I worked for them.”

Seagram’s had a ratings system for new make distillate that ranged from one to five, one being the worst and five being the best. For the last three plus years before Rutledge got to Four Roses the average score was one. By the third week of January of 1995, Rutledge was sending then plant manager Al Young up to the Seagram’s distillery in Lawrenceburg, Ind. with distillate samples almost daily for evaluation by Jim Warner and Pat Loach.

Rutledge was averaging 16 to 18 hours a day when the call finally came. “Jim said, ‘Guys, what are you doing down there? This is unbelievable. I haven’t smelled a distillate like this in years!’ And my heart jumped. But then he laughed and said, ‘I just wanted to call you and let you know you just had your first four-rated quality in over three years.’”

But the brand wasn’t out of the woods yet. Number crunchers in the parent company had all but decided that it would be a huge cost-savings measure to shut it down. The majority of what the Four Roses Distillery was doing at that point was making blending whiskey for Seagram’s Seven Crown domestically and Crown Royal Seagram VO in Canada, and they certainly had plenty of other facilities that could make it. Fortunately the corporate quality department stepped in and said we can’t afford to lose Four Roses because the quality is too good.

Rutledge and his team had done it. He was awarded the Seagram’s Top Quality Award. He tried to share the prize with the union stewards but was denied, so instead bought everyone at the distillery matching Four Roses jean jackets and used the remaining funds to stock the vending machines in the break rooms.

Changing the Course of Four Roses History

At this point Four Roses Bourbon still was mainly sold in Japan, but Rutledge was determined to bring it to U.S. markets. “When I got back to Kentucky, it became a burning passion to get Four Roses back in the United States. I didn’t hesitate. I pushed people. I would talk to people, directors of marketing and sales, all the time. If they called me about something I always managed to steer the conversation toward getting Four Roses back in the United States.”

He managed to get the Four Roses Single Barrel on the market in 20 states by 1999. And in 2002, when Kirin took over the business from Seagram’s, Rutledge finally got a chance to make his big move.

The first week of January 2002, the CEO and CFO of Four Roses as well as representatives from Kirin spent a week in Lawrenceburg at the distillery. ”At the end of the week they said, ‘Jim-san, we’ve been asking questions of you all week. Do you have any questions for us?’” Of course, the first thing he thought of was to try to remove the legacy Seagram’s blended whiskey from the lineup and bring the Four Roses bourbon home to the U.S. To Rudlege’s pleasant surprise, they accepted the idea. “It was years later one of the Kirin personnel told me, ‘Jim, they weren’t going to say no to anything you asked.’ He was always kidding with me. I said, ‘If I’d have known that, I’d have asked for a lot more money!’”

Rutledge began his uphill battle of replacing the old blended Four Roses with Four Roses Bourbon throughout the country starting close to home.

“We started Four Roses in Kentucky,” he recalls. “If we can’t be successful in our home of Kentucky, how can we be a success in California or New York any, anywhere in between?”

Over the next 11 years, Rutledge pounded the pavement bringing the story of Four Roses to bartenders, whiskey fans, and anyone who would listen. His work helped to usher in a golden era not only for the Four Roses brand but also for Kentucky bourbon as a whole, often appearing alongside other legendary bourbon distillers like Jimmy Russell and Booker Noe.

Retirement Doesn’t Always Mean Retirement

In 2015 Rutledge retired from Four Roses. Kirin wanted him off the production floor and on the road full time in an emeritus role with no meaningful tie to the distillery’s operations. But he wanted to continue his work as a distiller, so after leaving he quickly got back into the game. By February 2016 he had the opportunity to work on a project at Castle & Key for a Louisville philanthropist.

“I always told people I’d like to end my life leaning over a fermenter, checking the quality, smelling it, tasting it, you know, putting my finger in and getting too big a whiff of CO2 and it’s all over, you know, my life, career, and everything,” he laughs.

In addition to staying on the production side, Rutledge continued building his legacy by mentoring others. Dixon Dedman, founder of Kentucky-based 2XO Whiskey, has long looked up to Rutledge, and still calls on him for blending advice.

“We talked through the philosophy of blending and how things work, why things work, why things don’t work, and the mystery of why some things that should work don’t work,” Dedman says. “I consider him a mentor, my mentor. We had a connection, but he didn’t need to share the time, share the knowledge, share the wisdom with me that he did. I am eternally and forever grateful for that because he just really helped me figure a lot of things out.”

And that is a story that echoes across the industry. Rutledge is the kind of person who will always answer the phone — gatekeeping is not in his vocabulary.

In 2021, Pennyroyal Distillery co-founder Ross Hutchison began helping some friends build a distillery in Adair County, Ky. Eventually Rutledge visited the site and agreed to work with the company, which began by sourcing barrels of whiskey. Fortunately there were plenty of barrels available that Rutledge had distilled at Castle & Key that had reached maturity, so Echoes of Oak was born.

“I remember sitting in his truck and riding over there, and he was telling me some stories as if I didn’t know who he was,” Hutchison says. “I absolutely knew who he was and how important he was. But Jim just kind of nonchalantly will mention things and talk about various people he’s met or things he’s done in a casual way, not a boasting way.”

Rutledge is showing no signs of slowing down. He’s working where he can, lamenting the downturn of the distilling industry. But he says that if things turn around he’d love to be back in a distillery making whiskey again, a sentiment he says is echoing through all of the distilleries with paused production right now.

“No matter where I worked, there’s a lot of hard jobs, a lot of heartaches sometimes, but I love the industry,” Rutledge says. “And I’ll go as long as I can, as long as I have something to do. I hope I don’t run out of things to do.”
